data.title: Trichotillomania — viva
data.summary: Hair & nail disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Trichotillomania** (Hair & nail disorders)_

**Q1. Write a note on trichotillomania (PYQ).**
- Body-focused repetitive behaviour (DSM-5 obsessive-compulsive and related disorder) — recurrent pulling of one's own hair resulting in hair loss, with repeated attempts to stop and significant distress/impairment
- Two peaks: preschool children (habit, benign, often outgrown) and adolescents/young women (chronic, psychiatric comorbidity)

**Q2. Clinical features.**
- Bizarre, irregular-shaped patches of incomplete alopecia (often on vertex/frontoparietal of the side of the dominant hand) with hairs of varying lengths, broken stubs, no inflammation, scalp normal
- 'Tonsure' pattern (Friar Tuck sign — vertex loss sparing the periphery)
- Eyebrows, eyelashes, pubic hair may be involved
- Trichophagia (eating hair) → trichobezoar (Rapunzel syndrome — tail extending into small bowel) — ask about GI symptoms
- Associated: anxiety, depression, OCD, skin picking, nail biting, ADHD

**Q3. Trichoscopy and histopathology.**
- Trichoscopy: broken hairs at different lengths, flame hairs, V-sign (two hairs broken at the same level), tulip hairs, hook hairs, trichoptilosis (split ends), coiled hairs, black dots, haemorrhages; no exclamation-mark hairs or yellow dots (as in AA)
- Histology: increased catagen/telogen follicles, trichomalacia (distorted soft hair shafts), pigment casts, perifollicular haemorrhage, empty follicles, minimal inflammation

**Q4. Differential diagnosis.**
- Alopecia areata (smooth patch, exclamation-mark hairs, yellow dots), tinea capitis (scaling, KOH), traction alopecia, pressure alopecia, secondary syphilis, loose anagen syndrome, hair shaft defects (monilethrix, trichorrhexis nodosa)

**Q5. Discuss trichorrhexis nodosa (PYQ).**
- Commonest hair shaft defect: nodes (beaded swellings) where the cortex frays into brush-like fibres — 'two brooms pushed together' — hair breaks easily
- Acquired (physical/chemical trauma — combing, bleaching, straightening — proximal in Afro-textured hair, distal in others) or congenital (argininosuccinic aciduria, Menkes, trichothiodystrophy)

**Q6. Write a short note on Menkes kinky hair (PYQ).**
- X-linked recessive ATP7A mutation — defective copper transport (low serum copper and caeruloplasmin) → pili torti (twisted flattened hair), steely brittle hypopigmented hair, pudgy cheeks, hypothermia, seizures, neurodegeneration, death in early childhood; treat early with copper histidinate injections

**Q7. Management.**
- Non-confrontational explanation; involve parents (children); habit-reversal training (awareness, competing response) and CBT — first line
- Pharmacotherapy: N-acetylcysteine 1200–2400 mg/day (evidence in adults), SSRIs (comorbid depression/anxiety), clomipramine, olanzapine/aripiprazole (low dose), naltrexone
- Barriers: short haircut, gloves, bandana; psychiatric referral for chronic cases
- Childhood habit type often resolves spontaneously

**Q8. Classify alopecia (linked PYQ).**
- Non-scarring: AGA, alopecia areata, telogen effluvium, anagen effluvium, trichotillomania, traction (early), tinea capitis (non-inflammatory), syphilis, nutritional/ endocrine, hair shaft disorders
- Scarring (cicatricial) — primary: lymphocytic (DLE, LPP, FFA, CCCA, pseudopelade of Brocq), neutrophilic (folliculitis decalvans, dissecting cellulitis), mixed (acne keloidalis, erosive pustular dermatosis); secondary: burns, radiation, trauma, infections (kerion, favus), tumours, morphoea, sarcoid

**Q9. Trichoscopy signs in detail.**
- Broken hairs at different lengths, trichoptilosis (split ends), flame hairs (wavy proximal hair residues), V-sign (two hairs broken at same level), tulip hairs, hook hairs, coiled hairs, black dots, hair powder (sprinkled shaft fragments), absence of exclamation-mark hairs (seen in AA) — though overlap possible

**Q10. Histopathology findings.**
- Increased catagen/ telogen hairs, trichomalacia (distorted, soft hair shafts), pigment casts in follicular canal, perifollicular haemorrhage, empty follicles, no significant inflammation, normal follicle density

**Q11. What psychiatric comorbidities and treatments?**
- Comorbid anxiety, depression, OCD, skin picking, ADHD; treatment — habit reversal training (first line), CBT, N-acetylcysteine (1200–2400 mg/day), SSRIs, clomipramine, olanzapine/ aripiprazole in resistant; children — often self-limiting 'baby trich' with parental guidance

**Q12. What is the 'hair pull test' and 'hair window' in trichotillomania?**
- Pull test is negative (hairs firmly anchored); 'hair growth window' — shaving or occluding a small area shows normal regrowth when the patient cannot pull — confirms diagnosis

**Q13. What are the DSM-5 criteria?**
- Recurrent pulling of hair resulting in hair loss; repeated attempts to decrease/stop; clinically significant distress or impairment; not due to another medical condition or psychiatric disorder (e.g. BDD); classified under obsessive-compulsive and related disorders

**Q14. What is trichobezoar and Rapunzel syndrome?**
- Trichophagia (eating pulled hair) forms a hair-ball in the stomach (trichobezoar) — abdominal pain, vomiting, obstruction; Rapunzel syndrome — tail of bezoar extending into small intestine; needs endoscopic/surgical removal

**Q15. What is 'tonsure pattern' and 'Friar Tuck sign'?**
- Patch of hair loss on the vertex/crown with a fringe of normal hair at the periphery — typical of chronic trichotillomania (hair at the margins is harder to pull)

## Quick spotter facts
- Bizarre patch with hairs of different lengths, flame hairs and V-sign — trichotillomania
- Trichophagia → Rapunzel syndrome

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Psychocutaneous disorders; hair disorders). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
